extracted.intended_audience: journalists and reporters covering transgender people and related topics
extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style and safety guide for journalists reporting on transgender and gender-expansive people, covering language, sourcing, privacy, legal context, health care, sports, visuals, and related ethical practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying incarcerated trans sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Always identify sources as they wish, even if obtaining records on a person requires asking for their deadname.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider granting anonymity to trans sources in prisons and jails, especially those who are not openly trans, as they may be at substantial risk for violence or retaliation. Take extra care to obtain consent for ongoing communication and publication from incarcerated people, as most of their communications will be monitored by prison staff. Any communication with journalists may place incarcerated people at risk for retaliation. Additional resources cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider interplay between gender identity and carceral policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage should not conflate or generalize issues across subgroups (trans women, trans men, nonbinary) because the same policy may have different implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to avoid generalizing experiences of one subgroup when reporting on issues involving trans communities at large. Note how sex-segregated housing rules and other regulations may apply differently depending on identity. Additional resources cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language around transgender health care
rubrics_metrics.description: Health care that trans people seek out as part of their gender transition is a type of medical care; longer phrases like gender-affirming care are acceptable and sometimes preferable for specificity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use medically accurate names of surgeries and treatments where necessary. Use the language a person uses for themselves in direct quotes where possible; avoid asking grossly invasive questions or including unnecessary detail for shock value. Acknowledge that not all trans people experience gender dysphoria or receive gender health care; many never receive care due to cost, access, or choice. Explain when insurance, hospital policies, or state laws classify care as gender-related and how that affects access. Additional resources cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender-neutral terms in health coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Medically accurate language referring to humans and their anatomy is sufficiently gender-neutral for journalistic writing; do not invent neologisms over simpler neutral words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary to avoid 'women' or 'men' in medical contexts, but avoid equating gender and anatomy. Consider who is affected (e.g., people with ovaries, people with prostates). Terms like patients or people are often inclusive. Avoid using euphemisms like 'people who menstruate' as blanket replacements if inaccurate. Use less common terms (e.g., chestfeeding, birthing people) only in direct quotes from people who use them. Be cautious of misinformation about groups 'banning' gendered terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use gendered medical language
rubrics_metrics.description: Use gendered language when it accurately reflects the study or context (e.g., a study that only includes cisgender women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the word women is partially accurate but others may be included (e.g., transgender men, nonbinary people), consider phrasing like 'women and other patients.' Choose the most accurate, specific language appropriate to the research or dataset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether protected health information is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether asking about genitals, hormones, or medical procedures is necessary to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether similar information about a cisgender person would be relevant. Avoid asking invasive or irrelevant questions. See also guidance on asking irrelevant questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting on detransition and retransition
rubrics_metrics.description: Detransition has several meanings; do not assume it equals transition regret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify how an individual is using the phrase. Understand that people stop transitioning for many reasons besides regret (e.g., lack of support, resources, identity changes). Medical studies define detransition differently; when writing about related studies, understand their definitions and methods and relay that context to readers. Use terms like retransition carefully and according to the subject's usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hormone therapy reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precise terminology for hormone treatments and avoid crude binaries like 'male hormones' or 'female hormones.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to specific hormones where possible or use masculinizing/feminizing hormone therapy. Note puberty blockers are not cross-sex hormones themselves. Explain there is no singular model for hormone therapy—people have varied goals, durations, and dosing patterns. Avoid implying one standard pathway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproductive health language
rubrics_metrics.description: Use terms like reproductive health rather than gendered phrases like women's health when appropriate (abortion, birth control, menstruation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that such topics can affect trans men and other transmasculine people. Use medical terms (abortion, pregnancy, testicular cancer) for specificity where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports reporting: contextualize expertise and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not uncritically assume the stated rationale for a restriction on trans athletes is grounded in scientific fact; explain and contextualize the specific expertise of quoted sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether sources have relevant knowledge in sports medicine or scientific literature pertinent to transgender athletes. Prefer authors of scientific literature and athletic/regulatory bodies for technical questions. Prioritize talking to trans athletes themselves. Note proportionality—how many trans athletes are actually affected by regulations. Acknowledge that proposed regulations can impact funding and procedures for all players even if few trans athletes compete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive advantage in youth sports
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overstating competitive advantage claims, especially for non-elite-level sports where data is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both proponents and opponents rely on a small collection of studies focused on physiological indicators; there is little data directly comparing trans athletes’ performance to cisgender peers. Emphasize that elite athletes undergo different scrutiny and that younger athletes generally are not subjected to the same biological-factor focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting on testosterone-related regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering rules that use testosterone thresholds, explain how the rules work and their scientific limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that IOC and NCAA have shifted away from testosterone mandates but some bodies still implement them; some rules extend to intersex women. There is no straightforward 'normal' testosterone level for any gender and limited research on how testosterone affects trans athletes' elite performance. Provide context about variability and the limits of existing research.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Transgender athletes' is an umbrella term
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'transgender athletes' as a monolith: specific policies may affect different groups (trans women, trans men, nonbinary) differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depending on policy wording, laws may classify nonbinary athletes differently or base restrictions on legal sex markers; be precise about who a law or rule affects rather than using umbrella phrasing carelessly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'drag' and distinguishing drag performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use drag or being in drag to describe merely dressing in gender-incongruent clothes; do not call someone 'in drag' or a 'drag queen/king' if they are not a drag performer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many drag performers are cisgender; clarify and defer to the person's wishes about names and pronouns when in/out of drag. If not possible to speak to them, opt for using a drag/stage name over other names. Note ballroom performers and subcultures have complex gender concepts that may not map neatly to 'cis' or 'trans'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous focus on appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid focusing on a trans person's appearance in ways that call attention to assigned sex at birth or fetishize/exoticize them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid descriptors like height or voice pitch unless relevant and avoid labeling features as masculine/feminine/androgynous unless the person uses that language. Do not publish before-and-after transition pictures of someone (including public figures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting on histories and cultures of trans people
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid framing being trans as a new phenomenon or a fad; recognize evidence of trans people across time, ages, and cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide accurate historical context (e.g., transition-related medical care history) and avoid sensationalizing or misrepresenting changes in data-gathering as definitive population changes. Additional resources and books cited for deeper context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obituaries and deadnaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Never knowingly deadname a trans person in posthumous news coverage, including obituaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the convention of reprinting a birth name (e.g., 'Jane Doe, born John Doe, died Monday') as it is disrespectful. Handle posthumous legacies sensitively and consider writing around the deadname when necessary (example given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting on transgender asylum seekers and refugees
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask about gendered language, names, and how sources want to be identified; be mindful that language and culture may use different terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not translate terms without consulting the individual; check with sources before including last names as publication could jeopardize asylum. Do not assume someone seeks asylum solely because of identity; clarify details. Use UN and other ethical reporting resources cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting on sex work involving trans people
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide context about disparities and realities without stigmatizing sex workers; use respectful terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'sex worker' over 'prostitute' or 'escort'. Clarify names and pronouns; many use different work identifiers. Confirm what is on/off the record and respect safety concerns; some details may be okay within a community but not for publication. Additional resources cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same-sex marriage: use precise legal language
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'same-sex marriage' when referencing legal status rather than 'gay marriage' or 'same-gender marriage' where legal sex markers are relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that trans and nonbinary people's legal sex markers complicate how marriages are classified; be precise about which documents agencies defer to (driver's license, birth certificate) and the implications of X markers. Use language as precise as possible when reporting on laws/regulations based on legally defined sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'losing a loved one' cliche in coming-out stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not frame family grief as more central than the trans person's experience when covering coming-out stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons to 'losing a loved one' are inappropriate unless the trans person has died. Keep the focus on the subject's perspective and agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding and reporting on polling data about trans issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious with polls: quality varies and question framing can produce very different results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drawing conclusions beyond the specific question asked. Review sample size, weighting, and methods. Interview those who conducted the polls whenever possible. Note that different questions (e.g., support for transition vs. support for restrictive laws) produce different findings; be wary of question order and grouping effects. Additional resources cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscuring information in photography and visual media that could endanger sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how an image or video could put trans sources (or their loved ones) at risk, especially in places criminalizing trans people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be especially cautious with images of transgender children; consider techniques like silhouetting to obscure identity. Even 'public figure' status at a hearing may not imply consent for publication of name/likeness. Use conceptual imagery where centering a specific person's likeness could be dangerous or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain informed consent from subjects for photos in private contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask for and receive clear, informed consent before taking or publishing photos or videos in spaces with a reasonable expectation of privacy (e.g., medical clinics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If consent cannot be obtained or is denied, do not use the image unless there is an extremely compelling reason. The guidance also applies to embedded images from social media. Never republish sensitive medical photos without explicit consent; weigh news value carefully because images may be reposted as shock imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cutlines and identification in images
rubrics_metrics.description: In cutlines, include only information that can be verified about someone's identity; do not assume someone's presence at a trans-focused event means they are trans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ambiguity exists, use alternative descriptions (e.g., 'A protester at a rally for trans rights' or 'a person in a green wig'). In crowd shots, avoid identifying specific people or groups as trans unless the group is explicitly made up only of trans people; do not conflate drag performers or gender-nonconforming people with trans people without confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removing deadnames or misgendering from audio/visual material
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using portions of clips that include deadnaming or misgendering; in archival footage, censor by dropping the sound rather than 'bleeping'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let viewers/listeners know someone is being misgendered or deadnamed if the clip must be used, and drop out the sound for the offending words rather than bleeping. See 'deadnames' guidance for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use file photos with care
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful that file photos can become 'representative of transness broadly' and may mislead or put individuals at risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose more conceptual imagery (flags, statehouse B-roll, illustrations) when centering a person's image could misrepresent scope or localize violence. Avoid reusing specific portraits taken for one feature as generic art for unrelated trans stories. Maintain necessary context in cutlines if file photos are reused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for inappropriate stock images
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid stock photos that falsely imply medical abuse or are easily misconstrued in trans-related stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use generic images (e.g., crying child getting shot) that could suggest unrelated medical contexts (e.g., puberty blockers) unless accurate. Prefer stock images of models who are actually trans or nonbinary if people are shown; avoid models who merely 'look' stereotypically queer to illustrate trans topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology: avoid outdated or inaccurate labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate, respectful terms and avoid outdated or offensive labels (e.g., gender identity disorder, crossdresser used inaccurately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'cis' as short for cisgender but note some may object; use 'cisgender' rather than 'normal' or 'typical' when contrasting with trans. 'Crossdresser' is typically inaccurate/offensive when applied to trans people unless they self-identify that way. 'Gender identity disorder' is outdated—use 'gender dysphoria' in clinical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrimination terminology in legal reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Be precise when discussing discrimination: 'sex-based discrimination' and 'gender-based discrimination' can have different legal meanings depending on jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering U.S. federal law, 'sex-based discrimination' is an accurate umbrella term that federal courts have applied to discrimination against transgender people. State/local laws may call out 'gender-based discrimination' specifically; clarify language and definitions relevant to the jurisdiction. Outside legal reporting, use less technical language and focus on tangible effects (anti-trans laws, bills restricting bathroom use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'gender-affirming care' and related terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender-affirming care includes a range of medical and cosmetic procedures sought as part of transitions; the term is broadly interchangeable with related phrases but each has technical connotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that gender-affirming medical care may include counseling, puberty blockers, hormones, electrolysis, or surgery. Note related phrasing (transition-related care, transgender medical care, gender-related medical care) and that technicalities and connotations differ; refer to the 'language around transgender health care' guidance for more.
